title: M10; NGC 6254
caption: The globular cluster M10, imaged by the Burrell Schmidt telescope at Kitt Peak

recognition.text: Published in the NSF NOIRLab image archive. No published rating.

story: This picture shows M10, also catalogued as NGC 6254, a globular cluster in the constellation Ophiuchus. It lies close on the sky to another globular cluster, M12, and shines at seventh magnitude.
M10 measures about 70 light-years across and lies about 16000 light-years away. On the sky it spans roughly half the width of the full Moon.

A globular cluster is a dense, ball-shaped swarm of very old stars bound together by their shared gravity. The stars are packed most tightly toward the centre and thin out toward the edges. Clusters like this orbit around the centre of our Galaxy, often far above or below its disc, and because their stars all formed at about the same time, they serve as useful records of the Galaxy's early history.
scale: M10 is about 16000 light-years away and about 70 light-years across, according to NOIRLab.

understand.summary: A CCD camera on the Burrell Schmidt telescope at Kitt Peak recorded M10 in visible light; the filters and colour mapping are not published.
understand.eye: The camera's exposures gather far more light than the eye, resolving many of the cluster's individual stars.

explore: The picture was made from CCD images taken in June 1996 with Case Western Reserve University's Burrell Schmidt telescope, part of its Warner and Swasey Observatory, on Kitt Peak in southwestern Arizona, during the Research Experiences for Undergraduates program at Kitt Peak National Observatory.
alt: A round, densely packed cluster of stars that thins toward its edges.
